books.section: Topic 4.4 America on the World Stage, A. Trade, Diplomacy, and the Expansion of American Influence
Madison's Presidency and the War of 1812

stimulus.text:
Tecumseh, a Shawnee leader, spoke to William Henry Harrison, governor of the Indiana Territory, at Vincennes in August 1810:

“Brother, since the peace was made, you have killed some of the Shawanoes, the Winnebagos, the Delawares and the Miamis, and have taken our lands. . . . The way, and the only way, to check and to stop this evil, is for all the red men to unite in claiming a common and equal right in the land, as it was at first, and should be yet, for it was never divided, but belongs to all.”
stimulus.source_note: Tecumseh to William Henry Harrison, Vincennes, August 1810, as printed in Benjamin B. Thatcher, Indian Biography (1832); wording verified against Wikisource. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Tecumseh's main argument in the excerpt is that

options.text: the United States should pay Native peoples for the land it took
options.misconception: He rejects sales entirely; a better price would not satisfy him.

options.text: each tribe should make its own separate treaty with the United States and sell its own land
options.misconception: He says the opposite: no single tribe can sell what belongs to all.

options.text: the British should govern the Indiana Territory
options.misconception: He wants British help, not British rule over the territory.

options.text: the land belongs to all Native peoples in common, so no single tribe can sell it

rationales.A: Tecumseh does not ask for payment. He says the land “was never divided, but belongs to all,” so it cannot be sold at all.
rationales.B: Separate treaties are exactly what he opposes: he says the United States buys land from village chiefs “who have no right to sell.”
rationales.C: Tecumseh never asks Britain to govern the territory. His argument is about who owns the land, not who should rule it.
rationales.D: His claim is that the land “belongs to all” in common, so a sale by one tribe alone is not valid. Only all the peoples together could agree.
rationales.general:
1. Find his rule. The land “was never divided, but belongs to all.”
2. Apply it to the sales. If the land belongs to all, one tribe's chiefs cannot sell it on their own.
3. Put it together. His argument is about common ownership, not about price or who governs.
Background: Harrison had bought large tracts at the Treaty of Fort Wayne in 1809 from chiefs Tecumseh said had no right to sell.
Remember: when a speaker says land belongs to all, ask who he thinks may not sell it alone.
